and after an NTD-affected pregnancy, suggest that low maternal B12 status is an independent risk factor for having an NTD-
affected pregnancy. Such studies showed differences in NTD risk by maternal vitamin B12 status, measured as total circulating
B12 or as serum holotranscobalamin (holoTC) (the fraction of total B12 that is destined for tissue uptake and cellular processes
thus metabolically “active”). Also, lower amniotic ﬂuid B12 concentrations and lower B12 binding capacity have been reported
in NTD-affected pregnancies (Steen et al., 1998). The relevant studies with at least 50 NTD case mothers are summarized in Table 3.
These studies indicate that there is an approximately three-fold increased NTD risk for mothers in the lowest quartile or quintile,

compared to the highest, of blood B12 concentration. The reports that failed to show a relationship of B12 status with NTD were
either studies with low numbers (less than 50 case mothers) and therefore more likely lacked sufﬁcient statistical power to demon-
strate a signiﬁcant effect, or were from an area of low indigenous NTD risk (e.g., Finland). Although it has been suggested that low
concentrations of vitamin B12 may merely be a reﬂection of a low folate status, the analysis of data from studies that measured both
vitamins suggests that they are independent risk factors in NTD. Of note, one study found the highest risk of NTD in women who
were in the lowest quartile for both folate and vitamin B12 (Kirke et al., 1993).
